name: Bianca Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I direct an opera chorus, play piano for rehearsals, record vocal guides and coach five singers. I have a music master’s, and after thirty years I can hear when an alto is about to lose a phrase before she does. I like building the first chord out of a room of separate breaths; I dislike chasing rights on a guide reused without a fee.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner is a civil engineer and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and about ten months of expenses saved; my chorus and recording fees are high for this job, and several opera and theatre employers are nearby. I use AI daily to sort my own rehearsal notes, then check the score and keep singer audio off those tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that a faster rehearsal schedule helps if paid preparation and recording-use rates sit beside it. I would still hear every entrance myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booked opera run, five singers and my partner’s wage cover our mortgage. Ten months saved cushions an ordinary cancelled guide session, so I expect this plateau to be secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid chorus, piano, guide and pupil dates and ask for written preparation and reuse rates. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate and compare it with our mortgage and health before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the bookings on my desk. A singer’s breath is easy to miss on a tidy timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a reuse rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guide can be sold or played again after my first session, and I want that later use paid. I would ask the company to put it in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no pension estimate yet. My partner and I would read the actual figure before changing the calendar.

do: Keep **chorus and pupils** with written preparation and reuse rates.
Request **actual pension estimate**; compare with mortgage and health before retirement choices.
feel: I feel **calm** about current paid bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell singers that generated vocal guides can be fast but cannot coach a shaky entrance in the room. I would ask the company and union which live and reused recording hours still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides and later-use fees make about a fifth of my own income, and I expect some buyers to switch. Ten months saved lets me argue from a contract, but it does not make a lost reuse fee return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would count guide sales and keep paid chorus and five pupils. In disruption’s first year, if two monthly guide payments disappear, I would bring signed reuse invoices to the musicians union and request written live coaching, preparation and recording-use rates before renewing the opera agreement; I would budget only cleared fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a recurring slice of my own pay shrinking. A contract can price an entrance, but it cannot force a studio to order one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to make another guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI for notes, but singer recordings stay private without permission. I would play any changed passage myself before delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the union promise new sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It can press for paid terms with our invoices; a buyer must still book us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that thinking AGI by 2028 could make vocal guides before robot singers arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed paid rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide and reuse fees plus associated paid score preparation to end in 2028, removing roughly a quarter of my own pay. Guides and reuse alone are a fifth; the extra preparation makes the larger loss here. The live chorus may keep work longer, but ten months saved is search time rather than replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total guide, reuse and preparation invoices, keep signed chorus and pupil hours, and ask what a paid human director still does at nearby schools. In the first year after 2028, if those fees end, I would seek a posted paid school chorus-director role only if my music master’s and years leading singers qualify, its actual in-person coaching and rehearsal preparation are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces the loss with workable transport; I would keep opera and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real quarter of my pay going quickly. Many nearby employers help only when one posts paid human hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a director title be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would check the posted in-person rehearsal and preparation hours and the wage after travel. A title without paid singers is decoration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not wait for robot singers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company can stop buying guides in 2028. The card places capable robot singers about three years later, around 2031.

fieldNote: The **2028 guide loss** precedes physical robot singing around 2031.
A **school move** needs real paid human duties, accepted qualifications, after-travel net and a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera board that five years until thinking AGI around 2031 lets us settle recording rights and paid rehearsal terms. Robot singers around 2034 are a later question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to thin, yet live chorus work can still pay if the company signs for coaching and preparation. I would rather use my influence over a real agreement than buy another tool that cannot book a singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would take our guide and preparation invoices to the union and propose a two-season agreement paying live chorus coaching, rehearsal preparation, cancellations and recorded reuse. In the first year after 2031, if guide payments stop, I would keep paid opera and pupils and ask the union to check each cleared fee against signed terms; if live coaching hours also fall, I would seek only a posted paid school director role accepting my master’s and chorus leadership with paid in-person rehearsal work, written net pay after travel replacing the loss and workable transport, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible recording decline, though five years gives us time to negotiate. A signed live-coaching hour means more than a hopeful future use of my recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will the board sign a two-season deal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. The union can put our invoices on the table, but I will budget only a signed paid hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload rehearsal audio to bargain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use fee records, not a singer’s voice, unless the singer gives written permission for a particular use.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot singers around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask the opera board for written live and recorded-use fees this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late shows, but no retirement date follows without an actual pension estimate. Our current chorus and engineering wages cover the next few years; ten months saved does not price the whole decade of recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid chorus and five pupils, request my actual pension estimate and written reuse rates. In the first year after 2036, if guide and preparation fees fall, I would seek a posted paid school chorus director only if my music master’s and leadership qualify, real in-person coaching and preparation are paid, and a signed written net offer after travel replaces lost fees with workable transport; I would retain opera and pupils until that offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant guide income while our current wages pay the mortgage. I would read the pension figure before cutting a rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you name a retirement year now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual pension estimate, mortgage and health first. An age alone does not pay bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no school posts a role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid opera and pupils while booked and read other actual openings. I would not spend the reserve on a title that exists only in a forecast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide and reuse fees could end before another paid role starts. Signed live chorus dates, a real paid school post and written net wages after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a singer’s guide when the opera sells it a second time. A second use should make a second payment to the musician who made it.

headlineQuote: A second use should make a second payment to the musician who made it.
portrait: Bianca is a **senior opera chorus director** with a music master’s, high fees, recordings and five singers she coaches.
She has a **ten-month reserve**, engineer partner, grown children and mortgage, with many nearby music employers.
She uses **AI daily** for private score notes but insists on singer privacy and written recording reuse pay.
She seeks **collective paid terms** and would change roles only after a qualifying paid human offer replaces lost fees.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could end guides, reuse and preparation fees worth a quarter of her pay.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed chorus dates**, a real paid school post and written net wages after travel.
